Here is the only chart for this post: https://images.duckduckgo.com/iu/?u=http%3A%2F%2Frockhoundblog.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2010%2F05%2Fsubdivision_igneous_rocks.jpg&f=1

Igneous rocks are all cooled magma/lava. The intrusive rocks tend to be formed from magma, while extrusive rocks tend to be formed from lava. Yesterday I talked about Bowen's reaction series, and how minerals will sort themselves into different types of rocks based on the temperatures at which they solidify. This is the basic idea behind igneous rock classification.

Mafic = Magnesium + Fe (iron) rich

Felsic = Feldspar + Silicon rich

Heavy elements like magnesium, iron, and calcium are represented in mafic and ultra-mafic rocks, while lighter elements such as feldspars and silicons are found in felsic rocks. As an example, the felsic rocks are rhyolite (https://images.duckduckgo.com/iu/?u=http%3A%2F%2Fskywalker.cochise.edu%2Fwellerr%2Frocks%2Figrx%2F6rhyolite-gray1586a.JPG&f=1)) and granite (https://images.duckduckgo.com/iu/?u=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.stonekitchens.com%2Fproducts%2Fgranite%2Fslabs%2FCRANBERRY%2520BROWN.jpg&f=1)).

For the sake of argument these rocks have the same chemical makeup (they are from different areas, so they aren't exactly the same, but they are very similar). The only difference is that the rhyolite is micro-crystalline, while the granite has crystals visible to the naked eye. This is caused by differing rates of cooling. The extrusive rhyolite lava (magma at earth's surface) cools down a lot faster than the intrusive granitic magma (which cools while surrounded by insulating rocks). The crystals in rhyolite don't have as much time to get into an ordered lattice, so the crystals are smaller. Granite has more time to cool, so it's crystals are large enough to be seen with the naked eye. This is true across the board, diorite has visible clasts while andesite is for the most part microcrystalline (it's actually common to have some larger crystals in andesite, but they "float" in a micro-crystalline matrix). Gabbro is just the coarse grained version of basalt.

Ultra-mafic rocks are interesting. The extrusive version of peridotite is exceedingly rare since the interior of the earth has cooled too much to form an extrusive version. That means that any komatiite that is found on the earth is from back when the earth was hotter and more tectonically active (generally greater than a billion years old, but I'm not actually sure of the age of the youngest komatiite).

So that's it for igneous rocks. It's basically a matrix of chemical makeup and cooling rates.

From here I can segue into a few different topics. I can continue onto metamorphic and sedimentary rocks, plate tectonics, or I can go over volcanoes.

Quick clarification on igneous texture:

The difference between granite and rhyolite is in their matrix (the groundmass, or what the larger crystals "float" in)

Most rhyolites are "porphyritic", meaning that they have a microcrystalline (very fine-grained) matrix with crystals that are, in fact, visible to the naked eye (called phenocrysts) "floating" about, as you said. This happens because some crystals are able to form within the magma chamber (Bowen's Rxn!) but then an eruption causes the remaining uncrystallized magma to cool rapidly.

Granites are "phaneritic", meaning the matrix is composed of crystals visible to the naked eye, not just any crystal in general. There is no fine-grained material.

"Aphanitic" describes the strictly microcrystalline igneous rocks, including rhyolites. And when felsic magmas cool extremely quickly, crystal growth is minimalized and natural glass is formed = obsidian.
